summary: This memo describes the encoding used in email and network news messages in several Japanese networks, which use character sets that need several bytes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Japanese uses thousands of characters, far more than old email could carry. This paper explains the trick used to send them in messages.

questions: how are escape sequences used in iso-2022-jp
subtitle: Encoding for Japanese characters in email and network messages.

tldr.problem: Japanese text uses thousands of characters that do not fit in traditional ASCII-only email protocols. Early email systems could only handle 7-bit ASCII characters.
tldr.mechanism: ISO-2022-JP uses escape sequences to switch between ASCII and Japanese character sets (such as JIS X 0208). The message starts in ASCII, uses escape sequences to switch to Japanese, and returns to ASCII before the end of each line.
tldr.outcome: This allowed Japanese networks like JUNET to send Japanese text in email and USENET messages without modifying email protocols, and it is still widely used in Japanese IP communities.

today: RFC 1468 is an Informational RFC published in June 1993 and remains the standard for Japanese character encoding in email. It is still widely used in Japanese IP communities and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
RFC 1468 describes ISO-2022-JP, a character encoding standard designed to allow Japanese text in electronic mail and network news messages. The encoding was first specified and used in JUNET, the Japan Unix Network, and is now widely used across Japanese IP communities.

The key challenge that ISO-2022-JP solves is that Japanese writing uses Kanji (Chinese characters), Hiragana, and Katakana, totaling thousands of distinct characters. Traditional email systems could only handle ASCII, a 7-bit character set with 128 characters. ISO-2022-JP works within the 7-bit limitation by using special control sequences called escape sequences to signal when the text switches from ASCII to Japanese characters and back.
sections.eli5: Email used to only understand English letters. Japanese has way more characters than that. This encoding trick lets you tell the email system 'now I am writing Japanese' and 'now back to English' using special codes, so everything fits.

sections.title: Character Sets and Escape Sequences
sections.content:
ISO-2022-JP is built around the concept of switching between different character sets using escape sequences. An escape sequence is a short, fixed pattern of bytes that signals a mode change. The main escape sequences are:

  • ESC ( B (three bytes: 1B 24 42 in hexadecimal) switches to ASCII
  • ESC ( J switches to the Roman set of JIS X 0201 (Japan's variant of ASCII)
  • ESC $ @ switches to JIS X 0208-1978 Japanese characters
  • ESC $ B switches to JIS X 0208-1983 Japanese characters (the more common version)

The JIS X 0208 character sets contain Kanji, Hiragana, Katakana and other symbols. Each character in these sets takes two bytes to encode. ASCII and the Roman set use one byte per character.

The Roman character set of JIS X 0201 is mostly identical to ASCII, except that the backslash character is replaced by the Yen sign and the tilde is replaced by an overline.
sections.eli5: Think of escape sequences as language tags. You write a tag that says 'Japanese for a while' and the decoder knows to read the next bytes as two-byte Japanese characters. When you write 'back to English' tag, it goes back to one-byte ASCII.

sections.title: How ISO-2022-JP Encoding Works
sections.content:
A message in ISO-2022-JP always starts in ASCII. To include Japanese text, the sender inserts an escape sequence (such as ESC $ B) before the Japanese characters. Each Japanese character then takes two bytes. When the sender wants to return to ASCII or needs to end a line, they insert an escape sequence to switch back (such as ESC ( B).

Key rules enforced by the standard are:

  • The message must start in ASCII
  • Each line must end with a switch back to ASCII or the Roman set (that is, before the CRLF line ending)
  • The entire message must end in ASCII
  • JIS X 0208 characters must never be split across a line break

These restrictions ensure that the message remains a valid 7-bit text that can travel safely through any email system, even very old systems that do not understand ISO-2022-JP.
sections.eli5: The rule is: start in English, switch to Japanese whenever you need it, switch back to English at the end of each line and at the very end of the message. This way, old email systems see it as regular 7-bit text and do not break.

sections.title: Message Structure and Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC specifies the formal grammar for an ISO-2022-JP message. A message consists of headers (as defined by RFC 822) followed by one or more lines of text. Each line can contain a mix of single-byte segments (ASCII or Roman characters) and double-byte segments (JIS X 0208 characters). When switching between character sets, the appropriate escape sequence must be used.

The formal definition is strict to ensure interoperability: a segment is either a sequence of single-byte characters or a sequence of double-byte character pairs. The escape sequences must match the character set being used, and all control characters like ESC, SI (Shift In), and SO (Shift Out) have specific meanings. This level of formal specification allows independent implementations to work together correctly.
sections.eli5: The RFC writes down exactly what a valid message looks like, the same way a recipe writes down exact ingredients. This lets any programmer implement it and get the same result as everyone else.

sections.title: MIME Usage and Modern Application
sections.content:
ISO-2022-JP is used in MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) headers. A MIME email declares it is using ISO-2022-JP by setting the charset parameter in the Content-Type header: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-jp. Because ISO-2022-JP is already in 7-bit form, no additional Content-Transfer-Encoding (such as Base64 or Quoted-Printable) is necessary, which keeps the message compact and ensures it works with older JUNET software.

The standard also permits ISO-2022-JP to be used in MIME Part 2 headers (non-ASCII text in email headers). When used in headers, the 'B' encoding (Base64) should be applied for safety. Some systems do not distinguish between certain escape sequences (such as ESC ( B versus ESC ( J) for display purposes, but when relaying messages between systems, the escape sequences must be preserved exactly.
sections.eli5: Modern email systems tag the message with 'iso-2022-jp' to declare what encoding it uses. This signals to the receiver how to read the escape sequences and Japanese characters correctly.
